This document sets out the foundations of the Leadership for the Ecozoic (L4E) brand. It was drawn directly from the website Applied Archive Atelier designed for the initiative, and codifies the decisions already living there: the palette, the type, the linework and the editorial rhythm.

It is not an exhaustive representation of every brand element. As L4E grows, across campuses, cohorts and partners, this document should grow with it.

These guidelines are intended to help and inspire you as you bring the brand to life. Before creating new assets, consult them to make sure you’re on the right track.

Share this document with partner organisations, Fellows, writers and designers who may be creating work on L4E’s behalf.
We are a transdisciplinary learning community investing in emerging leaders committed to realizing an era of mutual flourishing among all human and non-human life.
Reflect our belief that a different relationship between people and planet is possible.

Reflect research that moves to action on the ground.
As our most recognisable element, the logo pairs a radial asterisk (part seed head, part root system) with a literary serif wordmark. It is rooted, quiet and unmistakably of the living world.

The asterisk is the shorthand for our brand. Its radiating stems echo seed heads, mycelium and the values diagram at the heart of the website.

Use it on its own only where the audience already knows L4E: as an avatar, a favicon, or a sign-off at the end of a document.

The logotype is set in Bradford LL Medium with −1% tracking. It is generally not used without the mark.

When writing the name in running text, use live type: Leadership for the Ecozoic in full on first mention, L4E thereafter. Never typeset the logotype yourself; always place the supplied artwork.

The lockup is the structured relationship between the asterisk and the logotype, and the most common use of the logo.

The horizontal lockup leads on desktop headers, footers and wide formats. The stacked lockup takes over on mobile, social and narrow placements, where the asterisk spans both lines.

The area around the logo should always provide ample space so the balance and wholeness of the mark are not crowded or constrained by external elements.

The minimum clear space is X, the height of the asterisk, on every side. No accompanying text, images or other logos should appear in this area.

Whenever possible, the logo should appear in Forest on Cream, the brand’s default pairing, used across the website header and footer.

Reverse to Cream on Forest for covers, dividers and moments of emphasis. No other colour combinations are permitted.

On photography, the logo always appears in Cream. Place it over the darkest, calmest area of the image (foliage, shadow, water), typically top-left where the site navigation sits.

If no calm area exists, choose a different image or crop rather than adding a scrim.

To ensure legibility, the logo should never appear smaller than the sizes shown.

Horizontal lockup: 160 px / 40 mm wide.
Stacked lockup: 100 px / 25 mm wide.
Asterisk alone: 16 px / 5 mm.

On mobile, the stacked lockup is used in the header at 181 px wide.

L4E is based at McGill within the Department of Anthropology. McGill University, an English-language public research institution founded in 1821, is located in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, or Tiohtia:ke, unceded Kanien'keha:ka territory. 

The university has a longstanding colonial history, including the use of money from the Iroquois trust fund -never repaid-to build its original campus. In the 20th century, some of McGill's downtown campus buildings were used for MK ULTRA psychological experiments, which survivors allege involved children, including Indigenous children, who did not survive. The presence of unmarked graves tied to these experiments is now the subject of dispute between McGill and the Kahnistensera (Mohawk Mothers). L4E acknowledges this institutional legacy and its harms. It operates in solidarity with the Kanien'kehä:ka and Indigenous communities globally.

Our palette is drawn from the forest floor: a deep green, a warm cream and a muted sage between them. Its restraint lets photography carry the colour.

Our primary palette is Forest and Cream. Forest carries every word, rule and outline; Cream is the ground of every page.

Together they pass WCAG AAA in both directions, so the pairing can flip freely between light pages and dark covers, dividers and footers.

The warmth of the cream is deliberate: it reads as paper, not screen, and keeps the brand closer to the archive than to the interface.

Sage is our secondary colour. It sits between Forest and Cream and is used for hairlines, meta text, captions and the rhizome linework.

Paper is a recessed surface for panels and image placeholders.

Neither should carry body copy. Sage on Cream reaches only 4.0 : 1, sufficient for large text only.

Shades extend the palette for interface states, charts and layered graphics. They are derived by mixing the base toward a deep forest shadow and toward Cream.

Use sparingly; the base values remain the default.

Whenever the colour system is applied, text must remain clear and legible.

Each cell shows which text colour may sit on that shade. Cream text is marked in the dark cells, Forest text in the light cells, where the pairing reaches at least 4.5 : 1, the WCAG AA threshold for body copy.

Where no “Aa” appears, the shade is for graphics only.
Top row: Forest shades. Bottom row: Sage shades.

This bar is measured, not prescribed. It counts 2,399 brand-coloured fills across the eleven desktop pages and ten mobile screens of the website.

Forest and Cream share the page almost equally; Sage supports at around one tenth. New work should keep roughly to these proportions.

Three themes cover every surface.

Light is the default for pages and long reading. Mid, on Sage, is for short moments of emphasis with large type only. Dark is for covers, dividers, the menu overlay and the footer.
Typography is the brand’s voice made visible: a literary serif for ideas and a quiet grotesk for information, set close, unhurried and in sentence case.

Bradford LL is used for headlines, statements, titles and the logotype. It brings a literary, archival voice.

Its italic is used within headlines to give a key phrase emphasis (“a paradigm shift”) and for the titles of publications, episodes and events.

Weights in use: Regular, Regular Italic, Medium (logotype only).

The serif scale, taken from the website and rationalised. Line-heights tighten as size increases; letter-spacing tightens to −2% at display sizes.

Mobile values are those set in the mobile designs.

ABC Diatype is our workhorse. It sets body copy, navigation, labels, bylines and every piece of interface text.

It is neutral by design, so the serif can carry the personality. Use Regular almost exclusively; Medium is reserved for small emphasis in dense UI.

Labels are set in uppercase at body size, never larger.

The sans-serif scale. 15 px is the desktop reading size of the website, deliberately small and editorial; it relies on generous space around it.

For long-form print, step up to 10–11 pt.

Three pairing rules carry the system:

1.  Roman with italic. A key phrase in a serif headline turns italic; never the whole line.

2.  Serif title, sans byline. Titles of work are serif italic; the author follows in Diatype, introduced by a small “by”.

3.  Label and rule. A small Diatype label (uppercase for categories) pairs with a Forest hairline to open each section.

Both examples are taken directly from the website.

Our graphic elements come from the living world: roots that wander, a radial that gathers many voices to one centre, and circles that hold each area of work.

The rhizome is a field of hand-drawn root and branch fragments. It recalls the underground networks that connect a forest, a metaphor for L4E’s community of practice.

Lines are single-weight strokes, never filled, never closed into shapes. They are always Sage or Forest on Cream, or Cream on photography.

The linework should feel found, not composed: let it bleed off the edges and leave large areas open.

Two placements are established on the website.

Over hero photography, the linework is Cream and drawn across the image like roots in water.

In the footer, it grows up from the bottom edge in Forest behind the sitemap and newsletter sign-up, closing every page in the same ground.

Our photography is documentary and unhurried. It shows real people in real places (rivers, fields, campuses, retreats) and lets the land be as present as the people in it.

Colour should feel natural and slightly warm, as if shot on film: greens lean olive, skies stay soft, highlights are never clipped.

A fine monochrome grain sits over every image. It unifies photographs from many sources (Fellows’ phones, partners, archives) into one recognisable family.
Here are some guiding principles when choosing or commissioning photography. They’re not hard and fast rules, but a starting point for images used across print and digital.
Show people together in the landscape, at human scale.
Capture community as it gathers: retreats, conferences, conversation.
Let seasons and weather be part of the story.
Give place its own frame: campuses, rivers, fields.
Avoid treatments that make the work feel artificial, corporate or cold. These examples are the website’s own photographs, pushed in the wrong direction.
Avoid monochrome. Colour is part of the place.
Avoid harsh contrast and blown highlights.

Grain is applied in Figma as a Noise effect:

Type: Monotone
Size: 0.5–1
Colour: Black, 15–40%
Density: 100%

Use the lower end on portraits and the higher end on landscapes. On the web, export with grain baked in; don’t simulate it with CSS.

To meet this moment, we must move beyond siloed knowledge, cultivate transdisciplinary thinking, and prepare leaders who are ready to tell a new story of a flourishing community of life. This deep transformation begins with how we learn, how we take responsibility, and how we relate to each other and the Earth.
We challenge academic institutions to respond more boldly to the scale and urgency of today’s ecological and social challenges.

Our Ecozoic Community of Practice connects PhD Fellows, Faculty, Research and Administrative Staff, Postdoctoral Fellows, Affiliates, Community Partners and Alumni, across universities, movements and contexts.
We are cultivating a new kind of academic and activist community that is both intellectually rigorous and emotionally resonant.
PhD Fellows’ research is transdisciplinary in approach while being grounded in the anchor disciplines of Ecological Economics at the University of Vermont and Anthropology at McGill University.

We aim to graduate “pracademics” - thinkers and doers equipped to boldly effect change. Our Fellows develop strong advocacy and communication skills, supported by partnerships with leading organizations and mentors.

We support PhD Fellows in developing strong advocacy, communication and participatory decision-making skills through in-person and virtual collaborations across campuses, including:

Courses
Research-to-action projects
Retreats
Collaboratories
Workshops
Creative media
Co-created publications and presentations
Governance circles
Together, we are prefiguring the Ecozoic era. Through retreats, collaboratories, filmmaking, writing, and more, we are telling a new story about humanity’s role in a healthier, flourishing world.

How can we transform global ecological crisis into a future where we humans thrive together with the community of life on our shared planet? What does it take to build a world rooted in justice and sustainability?

Our Ecozoic Community of Practice connects PhD Fellows, Faculty, Research and Administrative Staff, Postdoctoral Fellows, Affiliates, Community Partners and Alumni, across universities, movements and contexts.
We are cultivating a new kind of academic and activist community that is both intellectually rigorous and emotionally resonant.

To meet this moment, we must move beyond siloed knowledge, cultivate transdisciplinary thinking, and prepare leaders who are ready to tell a new story of a flourishing community of life. This deep transformation begins with how we learn, how we take responsibility, and how we relate to each other and the Earth.
We challenge academic institutions to respond more boldly to the scale and urgency of today’s ecological and social challenges.

We borrow the term Ecozoic from cultural historian Thomas Berry, who imagined a future era grounded in the mutual flourishing of human societies and the broader community of life. Building on the foundation of its precursor,
, we welcomed our first cohort of L4E PhD Fellows in 2018, and continue to welcome new cohorts to our two campuses every fall.

PhD Fellows’ research is transdisciplinary in approach while being grounded in the anchor disciplines of Ecological Economics at the University of Vermont and Anthropology at McGill University.

We aim to graduate “pracademics” - thinkers and doers equipped to boldly effect change. Our Fellows develop strong advocacy and communication skills, supported by partnerships with leading organizations and mentors.

We support PhD Fellows in developing strong advocacy, communication and participatory decision-making skills through in-person and virtual collaborations across campuses, including:

Courses
Research-to-action projects
Retreats
Collaboratories
Workshops
Creative media
Co-created publications and presentations
Governance circles
Together, we are prefiguring the Ecozoic era. Through retreats, collaboratories, filmmaking, writing, and more, we are telling a new story about humanity’s role in a healthier, flourishing world.
We are a transdisciplinary learning community investing in emerging leaders committed to realizing an era of mutual flourishing among all human and non-human life

Name places, people and practices. Prefer the specific river to “nature”.
“…located off the shores of Lake Champlain in Vermont…”
Acknowledge the crisis, then turn to what is being built.
“How can we transform global ecological crisis into a future where we humans thrive together with the community of life…?”
Speak of human and non-human life together. Use “we” and “the community of life”.
“…mutual flourishing among all human and non-human life.”
Use precise terms (transdisciplinary, degrowth) and explain them once.
“We borrow the term Ecozoic from cultural historian Thomas Berry…”
Name institutional histories and harms plainly.
“The university has a longstanding colonial history… L4E acknowledges this institutional legacy and its harms.”

Small choices carry the voice.

Use sentence case everywhere, including headlines and buttons.

Choose one spelling convention per piece and keep to it. The website uses US spelling (“realizing”).

Write “L4E” after the first full mention of Leadership for the Ecozoic.

Introduce people by name and role, never by title alone.
